episodes.170660: With an abundant amount of moisture in the atmosphere and the high pressure centered overhead contributing to slow storm motions, an active monsoon pattern continued on August 4, 2022. Scattered to numerous thunderstorms impacts much of northern and central New Mexico with heavy rain common in the more robust thunderstorms. The Calf Canyon burn scar was hit again with significant flooding observed in Rociada.
episodes.170661: A surge of deep moisture moved over central California from the southeast during the afternoon of August 4. This moisture interacted with a hot and unstable airmass which was in place over the area resulting in the development of numerous showers and scattered thunderstorms during the afternoon over the Sierra Nevada, the adjacent Sierra foothills and the mountains and deserts of eastern Kern County.  Some of the thunderstorms produced very heavy rainfall with amounts between a half inch and an inch of rainfall in a one hour period which prompted the issuance of thirteen Flash Flood Warnings and four Significant Weather Advisories during the afternoon.
episodes.170691: A west-to-east-oriented stationary surface front was draped across far-southern Lower Michigan, northern Lake Erie, and western New York during the early morning of the 5th. This front acted as a focus for the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms as the front interacted with moderate MUCAPE and DCAPE, and weak to moderate effective bulk shear over Lake Erie. One of these storms produced a gale-force peak wind gust.
episodes.170698: As the high pressure centered moved back to the east of New Mexico on August 5, 2022, the refocused the monsoonal moisture plume over the western half of the area. Plentiful amounts of moisture in the atmosphere still led to scattered thunderstorms across western and central New Mexico through the afternoon and evening hours. The Calf Canyon burn scar continued to be the most problamatic area for flash flooding and more reports were received in the Holman and Cleveland areas.
episodes.170742: Thunderstorms brought locally heavy rain to Talbot County during the late afternoon and early evening of August 5.  Rainfall totals were as high as 1.5 to 3.0 inches.
episodes.170743: Thunderstorms brought locally heavy rain to northern Ocean County during the late afternoon and early evening of August 5.  Rainfall totals were as high as 3.0 to 4.5 inches.
episodes.170794: Numerous showers and thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening of the 4th. Slow storm movement led to some instances of flooding and flash flooding.

episodes.170901: Thunderstorms ahead of a cold front produced numerous instances of gale to storm force winds over area waterways.
episodes.170907: A return of monsoonal moisture lead to numerous thunderstorm development during the afternoon and evening of the 4th. These thunderstorms were high-based and produced isolated severe downburst winds primarily east of the Caprock escarpment.
episodes.170911: An isolated thunderstorm developed directly over the Hart (Castro County) mesonet during the early morning hours of the 5th.  It began to collapse over the mesonet leading to a severe wind gust.
episodes.170940: Flash flooding occurred along Buckhorn Creek with impacted several sections along Buckhorn Road (LCR 44H). Numerous washouts were observed along Buckhorn Rd. from Ballard Rd to mile marker 30. An estimated 2-3 foot surge of water and debris was reported along Buckhorn Creek.  In Denver, a landspout briefly formed in an open field near Denver International Airport.  It did no damage.
episodes.171155: Clusters of thunderstorms moved into Delmarva from the west causing scattered wind damage across the eastern shore.
episodes.171157: Clusters of thunderstorms moved into Delmarva from the west causing scattered wind damage into southern Delaware.
episodes.171159: Heavy thunderstorms moved into eastern Pennsylvania producing locally heavy rainfall. One of the storms produced a lightning strike which struck a person.
episodes.171163: Scattered thunderstorms developed across the Delmarva peninsula producing some isolated heavy rainfall. One storm crossed into Sussex County from Maryland and produced some isolated wind damage in Delmar and another storm produced a lightning strike which struck a house west of Bethany Beach.
episodes.171165: Scattered thunderstorms developed across the Delmarva peninsula resulting in locally heavy rainfall and isolated wind damage.
episodes.171166: Training clusters of thunderstorms developed near the intersection of the sea breeze and an outflow boundary approaching from the south. This resulted in an area of heavy rainfall across northern Ocean, southern Monmouth, and eastern Burlington Counties which produced some locally significant flash flooding. Some isolated wind damage was also reported in northern Ocean County. Another cluster of heavy thunderstorms developed late in the evening in Mercer County and across the river in Bucks County, PA and tracked northeast producing locally heavy rainfall as well.
episodes.171251: Multiple locations reported a combination of brief heavy rain, flooding, or debris flows.
episodes.171275: A deep layer of monsoonal moisture pushed northwest and north into California, Sierra, and western Nevada in a southerly upper flow that marked the western margins of an area of strong high-pressure ridging into the Great Basin region.  Thickening mid-level moisture coupled with steep afternoon lapse rates and warmer surface heating initiated deep columns of slow-moving moisture-laden showers and thunderstorms with torrential rains over the 2021 Tamarack burn scar. This resulted in widespread flash flooding and debris flows in Alpine County CA that created a number of impacts. Rainfall rates of 2.22 inches per hour were observed during the peak of the storm in Markleeville, CA which corresponds to at least a 500 year recurrence interval and possibly 1000 year, per NOAA 14 atlas.
episodes.171276: A deep layer of monsoonal moisture pushed northwest and north into California, Sierra, and western Nevada in a southerly upper flow that marked the western margins of an area of strong high-pressure ridging into the Great Basin region.  Thickening mid-level moisture coupled with steep afternoon lapse rates and warmer surface heating initiated deep columns of slow-moving moisture-laden showers and thunderstorms with torrential rains over the 2021 Tamarack burn scar. This resulted in widespread flash flooding and debris flows in Alpine County CA that created a number of impacts. Rainfall rates of 2.22 inches per hour were observed during the peak of the storm in Markleeville, CA which corresponds to at least a 500 year recurrence interval and possibly 1000 year, per NOAA 14 atlas.
episodes.171528: A thunderstorm became severe over eastern Bennett and southeast Jackson Counties, then tracked southeast into Todd County. The storm produced large hail and some wind gusts as high as 80 mph.
episodes.171533: A thunderstorm briefly became severe over Mellette County, producing hail and wind gusts around 60 mph.
episodes.171534: A thunderstorm briefly became severe over eastern Jackson County, producing wind gusts around 60 mph east of Wanblee.
episodes.171868: Afternoon sea breeze thunderstorms produce gusty winds over the coastal waters around west central Florida and a waterspout offshore Hernando County.
episodes.171869: Afternoon thunderstorms produce severe hail near Charlotte Harbor in Charlotte County and lightning damage near Clearwater in Pinellas County.
episodes.172063: Hot and muggy conditions were in place on the afternoon of August 5th as a disturbance entered into the lower Ohio Valley. Showers and strong thunderstorms thrived on this day, moving in a northeast fashion from Central West Virginia up into the mountains. ||A 64 mile per hour wind gust was measured at the Charleston airport early that evening as a strong storm passed overhead. This same storm dumped a decent amount of rain in a short amount of time, which resulted in flooding downtown. As convection traveled into the higher elevations late that afternoon, several instances of flooded roadways and downed trees occurred.
episodes.172075: Slow moving pulse storms created flash flooding conditions across the region. The storms developed in a very moist, buoyant environment where 2000-3000 J/kg SBCAPE and 1.7-1.9 inch PW values, supported very efficient rainfall rates. Shear profiles were weak from the low levels to 300mb and created a 'pulse-type' behavior.
episodes.172086: A shortwave trough moved south from Missouri over parts of the Mid-South. Showers and thunderstorms slowly moved over the area, causing heavy rainfall resulting in flash flooding.
episodes.172087: A shortwave trough moved south from Missouri over parts of the Mid-South. Showers and thunderstorms slowly moved over the area, causing heavy rainfall resulting in flash flooding.
episodes.172131: Sea breeze conditions developed over the state in the afternoon hours with a weak background wind regime.  Heavy showers then formed over portions of Maui.  The rain caused small stream and drainage ditch flooding, and ponding on roadways.  There were no reports of serious injuries or property damage.
episodes.172164: Southeast steering flow focused the east coast sea breeze well inland into the afternoon where the merger of sea breezes and outflows occurred toward the I-75 corridor. Elevated DCAPE was near 1000 J/kg which promoted strong gusty winds in strongest storms.
episodes.172215: Storms with supercell characteristics at times developed in the heat of the afternoon ahead of a cold front, and continued to expand in coverage through the evening and overnight. Up to tennis ball sized hail was observed near the Faulkton area, along with sporadic thunderstorm wind damage. Localized gusts up to 76 mph were observed at and near the Watertown airport as well. After thunderstorms had largely dissipated, environmental conditions became favorable for additional severe wind gusts of around 60 mph (gravity waves). Overall rainfall totals neared 4 inches in a few spots including 4 miles north of Vivian (3.82 inches) and Summit (3.98 inches). Minor street flooding was reported in Aberdeen.
episodes.172318: Clusters of storms developed along a surface trough on August 5th and spread eastward into southeast Kentucky during the afternoon hours. One of these storms produced wind damage in Harlan County.
episodes.172389: Heavy downpours spawned from afternoon showers and thunderstorms across the Ohio Valley resulted in a local road to become flooded in Perry County.
episodes.172396: Strong thunderstorms ahead of a low pressure system surged through southwest Virginia on the afternoon of August 5th. These storms were able to produce locally strong wind gusts, which resulted in downed trees across Buchanan and Dickenson Counties just before the evening arrived. Storms were primarily driven by daytime heating and dissipated shortly after sunset.
episodes.172404: Oppressive heat and humidity and a very weak upper level disturbance triggered isolated to scattered severe thunderstorms in eastern Massachusetts in the mid to late afternoon. Locally heavy rain also caused some flooding.
episodes.172422: Showers and thunderstorms that developed on the hot and muggy afternoon of August 5th led to a few instances of flash flooding across southwest Virginia. Main impacts from these heavy downpours were flooded roadways during the evening commute.
episodes.172570: Several clusters of storms moved from southwest to northeast across East Tennessee, producing widespread wind damage in the form of downed trees.
episodes.172571: Several clusters of storms moved from southwest to northeast across East Tennessee, producing widespread wind damage in the form of downed trees.
episodes.172736: Continued stream of moisture across the region produced numerous pockets of heavy rain leading to flash flooding, mainly in Fremont County.
episodes.172829: A very small but stationary cluster of thunderstorms sat over the same area during the early morning hours. Isolated flash flooding occurred under this cluster. These storms were associated with a weak cold front that extended from Lake Michigan down into southeast Illinois.
episodes.172830: Two very slow-moving areas of thunderstorms crossed western Kentucky during the overnight hours into the early morning hours. These storms dumped up to 5 inches of rain in about 6 hours. Isolated pockets of flash flooding occurred with these excessive rain totals. The storms were associated with a weak cold front that extended from Lake Michigan south into the lower Ohio Valley.
episodes.172917: Strong heating during the afternoon created an unstable airmass with surface-based CAPE values in excess of 3,000 J/Kg across Tazewell County and the surrounding area, while precipitable water values varied between 1.6 and 1.8 inches.  One thunderstorm developed to the near Richlands at around 6:15 pm EDT and lingered for about 75 minutes before weakening. This storm produced prolonged rainfall rates of 3 to 4 inches per hour.  Runoff from this storm resulted in small stream flooding of tributaries of the Clinch River, including Little Town Hill Creek, which flooded across U.S. Highway 460 and Hillcreek Road.  MRMS FLASH (Flooded Locations and Simulated Hydrograph) data indicated a 3-hour Average Recurrence Interval between a 40- and 75-year event, while estimated rainfall was up to 1.8 times that of 3-hour flash flood guidance.  CREST (Coupled Routing and Excess Storage) Unit Streamflow in the area ranged from 300 to 500 cfs per square mile.
episodes.172927: Unstable conditions supported scattered showers and thunderstorms. A stronger storm passed through southern Broome County in Central New York and knocked down a tree onto a roadway just south of Binghamton. Small hail was also reported with storms this day.
episodes.173055: Slow moving thunderstorms produced locally heavy rainfall during the afternoon hours.
episodes.173119: Daytime heating and an unstable airmass produced widely scattered afternoon showers and thunderstorms. A few of these storms reached severe levels and generated damaging wind gusts.
episodes.173125: An upper level disturbance crossed the region during the peak heating of the day. The timing of these two events helped yield a generous coverage of showers and storms across the area, with a couple of storms becoming severe. Those that became severe produced damaging wind gusts. Lightning was also known to have struck a house and also a chimney.
episodes.173133: An upper level disturbance crossed the region during the peak heating of the day. The timing of these two events helped yield a generous coverage of showers and storms across the area, with one storm becoming severe. The storm that became severe produced damaging wind gusts.
episodes.173148: A surface trough off to the west slowly progressed eastward through the day. By the time it got to our area it was able to spark severe thunderstorms over southeastern NY that produced damaging wind gusts.
episodes.173149: A surface trough off to the west slowly progressed eastward through the day. By the time it got to our area it was able to spark severe thunderstorms over the waters that produced damaging wind gusts.
episodes.173237: An inverted upper trough extending from Central Louisiana into Deep East Texas became absorbed into a weak shear axis across Northeast Louisiana and East Texas on August 5th. These upper level features tapped into a very hot, moist, and unstable air mass with the aid of diurnal heating, with widely scattered showers and thunderstorms developing across East Texas and North Louisiana. Given the elevated nature of these storms, damaging downbursts resulted across the cities of Longview and Mount Pleasant, resulting in numerous trees and power lines downed with some damage to buildings before the storms diminished during the evening.
episodes.173324: A thunderstorm became severe near Big Piney, WY and produced damage.
episodes.173402: Storms moved southward across southern Missouri producing heavy rainfall and damaging winds. Flooding occurred on several low water areas.
episodes.173442: Scattered thunderstorms in advance of a surface trough produced gusty winds across portions of the Maryland Coastal Waters.
episodes.173526: Scattered severe thunderstorms associated with a surface trough produced damaging winds and large hail across portions of central and eastern Virginia.
episodes.173528: Isolated severe thunderstorm associated with a surface trough produced large hail across portions of the Lower Maryland Eastern Shore.
episodes.173529: Scattered thunderstorms associated with a surface trough produced heavy rain which caused flash flooding across portions of central and south central Virginia.
episodes.173530: Scattered thunderstorms associated with a surface trough produced gusty winds across portions of the Chesapeake Bay.
episodes.173789: Broad east to southeast flow advected in monsoon moisture, which fueled thunderstorms over southeast California. Several storms produced flash flooding.
episodes.173790: Broad east to southeast flow advected in monsoon moisture, which fueled thunderstorms over southern Nevada. Several storms produced flash flooding.
episodes.173996: A very hot and unstable airmass was in place across the region on August 4th with heat index values reaching into the mid-90s during the afternoon hours. A weak mid-level trough provided the region with enough instability for thunderstorms to develop across the Connecticut River Valley during the late afternoon.  The storms moved east through the early evening bring strong damaging wind gusts to parts of Southern and Central New Hampshire.
episodes.174031: A very hot and unstable airmass was in place across the region on August 4th with heat index values reaching into the mid-90s during the afternoon hours. A weak mid-level trough provided the region with enough instability for thunderstorms to develop across the Connecticut River Valley during the late afternoon. The storms moved east through the early evening bring strong damaging wind gusts to Oxford County before the storms weakened and moved east.
episodes.174032: A very hot and unstable airmass was in place across the region on August 5th with heat index values reaching into the mid-90s during the afternoon hours. A weakening frontal boundary sagged south across the region that interacted with a sea breeze front that caused enough lift to trigger isolated thunderstorms across the NH/MA border region.  A strong microburst due to the precipitation loading and dry planetary boundary layer caused localized damaging winds, especially in the Hollis area.

Significant flash flooding was reported across the western side of Franklin County. Water was over Route 14 in multiple locations west of Christopher. Water was over Route 184 in multiple locations north and south of Mulkeytown. Many rural roads were completely impassable. A Cocorahs observer at Christopher measured 5.11 inches of rain over 48 hours.

The Cooperative Weather Observer in the Town of Richlands observed a 24-hour rainfall amount of 2.07 inches, caused by a thunderstorm.  This was a new daily record for this station and the 2nd-highest 24-hour total during the month of August.

A COOP Observer from Moorman Ranch reported 24-hour rainfall at his location of 2.94 inches. He added between 16 and 1800LT a portion of his mountain/hillside came down due to the heavy rain, and he had to clear/repair his driveway with his excavator. Some additional details of note; of the 2.94 inches that fell that Friday, 0.54 inches fell between 2000 that evening and 0400LT the next morning. It was the most rain our observer has seen in a 24-hour period in his 30 years in the area.
Every road in Death Valley National Park was closed, and several were damaged by flooding as well. One vehicle was stuck in mud near Stovepipe Wells, and the Cow Creek water system was broken.
A waterspout was reported by a Galveston County Emergency Manager just northeast of Bayou Vista.  It lasted less than a minute and no spray ring was visible.
